articles.title: Why has an NYT report on Iran’s dams ignited fierce pushback?
articles.summary: The NYT faces backlash over report suggesting a possible link between Iranian dams and underground missile facilities.
articles.body:
A New York Times (NYT) story suggesting that some of Iran’s dams and water infrastructure may have been built to support the country’s missile programme has sparked fierce backlash, with commentators warning the report could help justify further attacks on civilian facilities.

The controversy comes as Washington threatens renewed military action against Iran, following months of war that have already left the country’s energy facilities, bridges, water infrastructure and other civilian sites damaged.

“The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said in a post on X.

The newspaper has defended its reporting, insisting it accurately represented the views of its experts.

However, several experts quoted by the publication have publicly challenged the implications of the investigation, questioning the evidence behind the proposed link between dams and military installations.

The controversy has also revived memories of the NYT’s reporting in the lead-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, when the paper’s journalists helped amplify claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction that later proved unfounded.

Published on Tuesday, the story, headlined “War May Answer Longtime Riddle of Iranian Dams Built for No Clear Reason”, examined whether Iran’s extensive network of dams, pipelines and water-transfer projects could be connected to its underground missile programme.

The report cited researchers who observed geographical similarities between the locations of dams and sites targeted by US and Israeli air strikes.

According to the report, some of the water and military experts the NYT spoke to concluded that the “water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup”.

However, the newspaper itself acknowledged, “Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.”

Critics fear that portraying dams as potentially serving military purposes could provide a justification for attacking infrastructure essential to millions of civilians.

US-Israeli attacks on Iran since February 28 have damaged oil facilities, power plants, water reservoirs, bridges, hospitals and other civilian infrastructure.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened further attacks, saying last week that key Iranian infrastructure could be destroyed within three days.

Political analyst Rami Khouri called the NYT report “troubling”, saying it reaffirmed his concerns about US mainstream media being “complicit in the US-Israeli criminal attacks on Iran, just as it was during the war on Iraq decades ago and the ongoing genocide in Gaza”.

“The telltale sign of non-credible wobbly journalism is when conditional words like ‘speculative’, ‘suggestive’, ‘may have developed’, ‘may shed light’, ‘suspect’, and ‘long-term riddle’ occur more often than any definitive, evidence-based facts.”

Khouri said it was “not definitive and verified reporting” and “another attempt to support the US-Israeli urgency to find any reason to carry out more war crimes against Iran” by attacking critical infrastructure.

“Another sad day for US mainstream journalism,” he added.

Aside from online criticism from readers and commentators, experts cited in the story have themselves come out against aspects of the report.

Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University’s water institute and a former senior Iranian environmental official, one of the experts cited in the story, challenged the report’s reasoning.

“Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” he wrote on X.

“Even those who attacked Iran have not made such claims linking dams to missiles! This reductionist, sensational narrative is irresponsible journalism with potentially dangerous consequences for civilian water infrastructure. The New York Times should know better.”

Madani also questioned the newspaper’s claim that seven experts had supported its analysis. “I’m one of the people quoted in the article, but my comments had nothing to do with dams or missiles!” he added.

Nima Shokri, a water-security expert at Hamburg University of Technology, whose research featured prominently in the investigation, also issued a clarification.

“The proximity of dams to military targets does not establish why those dams were built, nor does it justify attacks on them,” he said on X.

A third researcher quoted in the article echoed Shokri’s comments.

“I fully agree [with Shokri],” Amir Aghakouchak, a water expert at the University of California, Irvine, wrote on X, sharing Shokri’s X post.

“Dams and water infrastructure are essential to civilian life and must never become targets of military attacks. Regardless of their location or potential strategic significance, their primary roles in water supply, food security, energy, and environmental sustainability must not be overlooked. Protecting these critical resources should be a priority, regardless of politics or conflict.”

The newspaper rejected accusations that its investigation could provide a pretext for military attacks.

“Our report on Iranian dams accurately cited research and analysis by seven international experts on Iran’s environment and military presence,” spokesperson Nicole Taylor said.

She added that the NYT’s journalists had sought to explain Iran’s infrastructure investment and the effects of US and Israeli attacks on civilians.

“Framing the independent reporting as a pretext for violence is dangerous,” Taylor said.

One of the story’s co-authors, Sanam Mahoozi, said that “neither I nor our report endorses or justifies attacks on dams or other infrastructure”.

“As a journalist, I welcome rigorous, constructive criticism, but I hope some users will critique the report fairly, based on what was actually written,” she posted on X. The story was co-written with Erika Solomon, the NYT bureau chief for Iraq and Iran.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the allegations as “rubbish”, accusing what he suggested was pro-Israel media of promoting narratives reminiscent of the run-up to the 2003 US invasion of Iraq.

“Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda, especially with Israeli fingerprints all over it,” he wrote on X.

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, accused the newspaper of preparing the ground for further attacks on civilian infrastructure.

“New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” he posted on X.

Why are people questioning the NYT’s credibility?

The controversy has revived widespread criticism of the newspaper’s reporting before the US-led invasion of Iraq , when claims about Saddam Hussein’s alleged weapons of mass destruction helped build public support for war.

Judith Miller, a former NYT journalist, was among the reporters whose coverage amplified claims about Iraq’s weapons programmes that subsequently proved unfounded.

In September 2002, Miller co-authored a report claiming Iraq had intensified its pursuit of nuclear weapons, citing US officials who alleged that Baghdad was seeking aluminium tubes for uranium enrichment.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney cited the newspaper’s reporting on aluminium tubes to bolster President George W Bush’s administration’s case against Iraq. The claims were later discredited.

Two months after the invasion of Iraq began in March 2003, Miller co-authored a report citing that US intelligence agencies had concluded that two mysterious trailers found in Iraq were mobile units to “produce germs for weapons”.

However, a year after the US war on Iraq began, the NYT acknowledged serious shortcomings in its reporting on the build-up to war, including its reliance on Iraqi defectors and exiles seeking regime change.

“We have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been,” it said.

articles.title: The outages America has suffered weren't an attack, but the next failure could be
articles.summary: The FAA ground stop, Microsoft outage and Chase bank outage stem from fragile systems, not sabotage, officials say. Here's what the cluster of outages really reveals.
articles.body: The recent string of outages is a statistical cluster that exposes real fragility, not coordinated sabotage — but it should still wake us up. Over the past week, Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, went dark worldwide after a latent defect from a July network update surfaced under heavy load. Next, the FAA ordered a rare nationwide ground stop after routers at sites in Arkansas and Texas overwhelmed aging air traffic control systems. Then Chase and other banks saw transaction slowdowns from a software bug. United delayed departures because of an internal system failure. And finally, reports emerged of disruptions to the NSA’s classified internal network. Officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have stated they are highly confident these were unrelated technical issues, not a cyberattack. But we humans are wired to seek patterns. Events this close together feel ominous. In this case, the evidence points to a predictable downside of efficiency: concentrated cloud computing dependencies and incompletely tested updates that create single points of failure across email, aviation, finance and more. TECH OUTAGES: LATEST ON MICROSOFT, BANK DISRUPTIONS AND FBI ASSISTANCE IN FAA REVIEW That does not mean the threat is imaginary. If China or Russia decided to inflict serious damage, we would not experience scattered inconveniences. Electricity would fail, water systems would stop, banking and payments would freeze, and cell networks would go dark — all at once, like a sudden thunderclap. Such an attack would almost certainly accompany or immediately precede kinetic action, most obviously a Chinese move against Taiwan, intended to slow or deter a U.S. response. Even Iran, North Korea or elements of the Mexican narcostate have some capacity to harm our critical infrastructure, with Iran being the prime suspect in water system attacks over the past few months. TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS Further, hostile nations do probe, looking for vulnerabilities. They may even conduct small-scale attacks to test response times. And, of course, there are gray-zone operations that offer significant asymmetric advantages and plausible deniability while imposing costs (economic, psychological and diversion of defensive resources) without crossing into open war. The recent attacks on industrial food freezers and blood banks in Europe and on U.S. military bases are examples of this, with the Russians as likely culprits. China has already laid the groundwork. Volt Typhoon, assessed as linked to the People’s Liberation Army, has pre-positioned access inside U.S. critical infrastructure — energy, water, transportation and communications — with the goal of enabling disruption or destruction in a crisis. Salt Typhoon, tied to China’s Ministry of State Security, has focused on intelligence collection, penetrating telecommunications networks to intercept communications and metadata at scale. One prepares to break things; the other listens in on us. An example of the former was discovered during the first Trump administration when a kill switch was found in a high-voltage transformer imported from China. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY Closer to home, the Mexican government under MORENA and President Claudia Sheinbaum increasingly frames relations with the United States in terms of a righteous struggle against "Norte Americanos." U.S. efforts to arrest high-ranking narcotraffickers on Mexican soil or destroy drug production facilities are treated as grave threats to sovereignty that require an answer. Mexico’s military (SEMAR and SEDENA) has acquired roughly 2,400 short-range intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and attack drones while building domestic manufacturing capacity, according to Ammon Blair, senior fellow at the Texas Public Policy Foundation. Officials have signaled interest in longer-range systems as a deterrent, putting U.S. infrastructure such as the electric grid and refineries at risk — precisely the lesson of drone warfare in Ukraine. The United States — federal and state governments, as well as private industry — is beginning to address these critical vulnerabilities. WATCH: DHS ISSUES STARK WARNING AFTER 300 ‘HOSTILE’ CARTEL DRONES DETECTED AT SOUTHERN BORDER The Department of War is finally starting to learn to use our counter-drone technology along our 1,954-mile border with Mexico. State governments are taking stock of their vulnerabilities in the event of a conflict across the Pacific. And industry is stepping up to the challenge of reshoring critical manufacturing capacity. One such vital component is the high-voltage transformers that make our electric grid possible. Essential to move electricity from power plants to homes, factories and data centers, these massive transformers are mostly imported (often from China) with lead times of two to four years. Roughly 70% of America’s existing units are more than 25 years old. Demand is exploding from data centers, electric vehicles and industrial growth. Startups such as Resolute Grid in Austin, Texas, are responding with domestic production. Many of its engineers are Tesla and SpaceX veterans who could have retired after those companies’ successes; now they are applying the same urgency to building large transformers that can be delivered in months rather than years. The firm’s CEO, Marcus Owenby, noted, "Resilience isn't just keeping the lights on. It’s how fast you can replace what breaks." Because without power, water, fuel, communications and finance all fail. THE MACHINES THAT KEEP AMERICA ALIVE ARE FAILING. WE FORGOT HOW TO REPLACE THEM Domestic manufacturing, strategic stockpiles, faster permitting and a clear preference for American production over adversarial supply chains are practical steps, not abstractions. The recent outages are not the opening shots of war. They are a reminder that complex, efficient systems fail and that determined adversaries have both the intent and the access to make failures far worse. Preparation, not panic, is the rational response. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Keep a modest amount of cash on hand; ATMs and card networks will not work if the systems behind them fail. Store water and rotate it; in a pinch, the water in a toilet tank is usable. Maintain a two-week supply of dried goods (rice, beans) and canned food so your family does not immediately become a burden on overwhelmed local and state resources. Buy a shortwave radio and a hand-crank or solar charger. If you can, own or share access to a generator. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Resilience is built by people who treat unglamorous bottlenecks — transformers, tested software, diversified supply chains, personal preparedness — as problems worth solving. The engineers in Austin who stayed in the fight instead of walking away understand that. The rest of us should, too. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM CHUCK DEVORE

articles.title: Police treating 'targeted' shooting of woman as attempted murder
articles.summary: The 27-year-old, who was shot in Glasgow on Monday night, is in hospital in a critical but stable condition.
articles.body:
Police are treating the shooting of a woman in Glasgow on Monday night as attempted murder.

The 27-year-old was taken to hospital after emergency services were called to Eynort Street in the city's Lambhill area at about 23:45.

The victim suffered serious injuries and is in hospital, where she is in a critical but stable condition.

Police Scotland described the attack as being "an extremely reckless act with no regard for the safety of the local community".

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The Sun newspaper earlier reported the victim is the partner of a gangster who has been targeted over drug debts. There is no suggestion the victim herself is involved in organised crime.

Det Ch Insp Jennifer McCulloch, from Police Scotland's major investigation team, said: "From our inquiries so far, we believe this was a targeted attack.

"However, this was an extremely reckless act, with no regard for the safety of the local community, and I want to make it clear this behaviour will not be tolerated.

"A young woman has been left with serious injuries and it is vital we find whoever is responsible as soon as possible."

Det Ch Insp McCulloch said there were other family members within the household at the time at the attack, but none of them were reported to be injured.

The force said it could not confirm the identity of the woman yet.

She added that the force is "following a number of significant lines of inquiry" and anyone with information on the attack should contact Police Scotland .

She also said "forensic opportunities" were being looked at by officers.

Detectives have set up a dedicated portal where information can be submitted anonymously and a heavy police presence remains in the area, with both uniformed and plain-clothed officers.

Lambhill is between Milton and Possil and the areas have seen violence involving gangs in the past.

A garage in Lambhill was where 21-year-old Michael Lyons was shot dead in 2006 and two others were injured.

The killing was part of the feud between the rival Daniel and Lyons families and the garage itself, now under a different name, was firebombed last year .

Supt Jackie Dunbar added: "This was a shocking incident for the local community in Lambhill, and I completely understand there will be concerns for those living in the area.

"But please be assured we are doing everything we can to identify and trace those responsible.

"High visibility patrols remain in the area and there will be an increased police presence as our investigation continues.

"If anyone has any concerns, or information, please speak to these officers."

articles.title: Tim Hortons accused of sharing user data with firm linked to Israeli army
articles.summary: Research into Tim Hortons’s app finds that it began transmitting information to Forter as soon as it opened.
articles.body:
The application of the popular Canadian coffee chain Tim Hortons has been sharing sensitive user data with Forter, an Israeli cybertechnology company founded by former members of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200 intelligence division, according to a Canadian advocacy group.

Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME) identified Forter as the third-party company receiving data from the app after a recent investigation by the CBC News broadcaster that raised concerns about the app’s data collection and sharing practices.

CBC News did not identify the recipient in its report.

The CJPME said on Tuesday that it contacted Joel Reardon, a computer science researcher at the University of Calgary whose findings informed the CBC investigation, to establish the identity and location of the company.

The research into Tim Hortons’s app found that it began transmitting information to an overseas third party as soon as it was opened.

The data included unique device identifiers, camera specifications, lists of device sensors, and the names of users’ ringtones and alarm sounds. It also included the names of nearby wi-fi routers, which Reardon told the advocacy group could be used to determine a user’s location.

Researchers said the information could be used to create a digital fingerprint of individual devices.

Israel has been facing growing international isolation over its genocidal war on Gaza, pogroms in the occupied West Bank and the occupation of southern Lebanon.

Tim Hortons said its app collects information for fraud prevention, account protection and payment abuse prevention and not marketing or advertising. The company also said neither it nor the third-party recipient of its app data sells users’ personal information.

Forter’s founders – Michael Reitblat, Liron Damri and Alon Shemesh – are alumni of Unit 8200, Israel’s signals intelligence and cyberwarfare division. The company says it uses machine learning technology to identify potentially fraudulent transactions, flaunting that its expertise draws from Israeli military intelligence.

Unit 8200, the largest single military unit in Israel, has faced scrutiny over its role in mass surveillance of Palestinians in occupied territory.

Microsoft last year barred the unit from using its technology after discovering that its systems had been used for surveillance operations against Palestinians.

“Canadians ordering coffee should not have their unique and sensitive user data shared with an Israeli cyber-tech company whose infrastructure was built by alumni of a foreign military intelligence agency engaged in human rights violations,” said Michael Bueckert, the CJPME’s vice president.

“The company’s ties to an Israeli military unit that oversees the mass surveillance of Palestinians pose significant ethical issues, raising alarm bells for anyone concerned about cyber-security. Tim Hortons must cut ties with this company immediately,” he added in a statement.

articles.title: Surfing legend found stabbed to death under bed – girlfriend accused of letting thugs in to wipe him out
articles.summary: Kurt Van Dyke's girlfriend and a man were arrested in Costa Rica over the surfer's murder, as the OIJ claims she helped armed attackers enter.
articles.body: A legendary California surfer's former girlfriend was among the two people arrested in Costa Rica in connection with his murder. Kurt Van Dyke, 66, was found dead in February inside his apartment in the Costa Rican town of Hone Creek, Cahuita, Limón. He was found with signs of asphyxiation and multiple stab wounds, local authorities said at the time. The Costa Rica Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) said Van Dyke's girlfriend, only identified as Arroyo, 31, helped armed attackers get into the apartment on Feb. 14, according to La Nación. A 34-year-old man identified as Gutiérrez was also arrested on Thursday morning. Van Dyke was found dead underneath a bed and wrapped in a sheet with several stab wounds. CALIFORNIA SURFER MURDERED IN APPARENT ROBBERY AT HIS HOME IN COSTA RICA: REPORTS Police in Costa Rica believe both planned a robbery against Van Dyke and wanted to steal the bank card codes associated with the hotel he owned in the country. During the raids on Thursday morning, police seized a cellphone and a vehicle allegedly used during the crime, as well as other items relevant to the investigation. SEND US A TIP Initial reports described the incident as a home invasion in which several men stormed the property and bound Arroyo's hands and feet. Arroyo told police the attackers had restrained her and fled with valuables, but investigators now believe her account was part of a cover story. Officials believe the gang staged Arroyo's car theft to make it look like a robbery, which authorities say supports their theory that Arroyo helped plan the attack. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Arroyo and Gutiérrez were referred to Costa Rica’s Public Ministry, the agency which will decide if they face charges. articles.title: Local legend Reading Elvis, known to thousands, dies aged 77
articles.summary: David Allon, a lifelong fan of the King of Rock and Roll, was often spotted in Reading town centre.
articles.body:
A local legend known to many thousands as Reading Elvis has died aged 77.

David Allon, a lifelong fan of the King of Rock and Roll, was often spotted in Reading town centre with his prized Elvis records or wearing a Presley T-shirt.

He turned on the town's Christmas lights in 2016 and hosted a DJ set at the Readipop festival in 2018.

Friend Trevor Absolom said news of Allon's death had led to "an unbelievable outpouring of love and affection over the last 24 hours".

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

He added: "I've lived in Reading all my life and I think most people who have know David or know of David. The one person who probably didn't realise how much he was liked was David.

"It probably took the Christmas lights event for him to know that everyone loved him. That day was incredible. For that one day he was Elvis."

Pete Wheeler, Reading charity Readipop's marketing director, said he "lit the place up" during the set at the festival.

"He was showing how much those tunes meant to him in the most visible way and it was beautiful. We feel privileged to have had him involved," he added.

Wheeler said Allon would line the route of the annual Reading Half Marathon and would give the runners a morale boost near Prospect Park.

Reading-based Elvis tribute act Paul Rouse said Allom was a "lovely guy".

"Everyone is saying exactly the same thing: it's the loss of a legend. I've known him to say hello to for about 40 years.

"He was just incredibly famous – you'd walk by and he always had an Elvis calendar or an album or a book. He always had an Elvis T-shirt – he must have had about 50 T-shirts over the years."

articles.title: 3,300-year-old bronze sword emerges from Italian lake and still has a 'sharp edge'
articles.summary: Archaeologists recovered a 3,300-year-old bronze sword from Lake Mezzano, a volcanic lake in Italy, and it's still sharp after 33 centuries underwater.
articles.body: Italian officials recently announced the remarkable discovery of a 3,300-year-old bronze sword in a volcanic lake — and it's still sharp, roughly 33 centuries later. The discovery, made at Lake Mezzano, was announced by the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria (SABAP-VT-EM) earlier in October. Lake Mezzano — once the crater of an ancient volcano — is located in central Italy's Lazio region, near the town of Valentano. STUDENT 'ACCIDENTALLY' FINDS 'EXTREMELY RARE' CRUSADER-ERA SWORD AFTER CHASING OFF SUSPECTED THIEVES Archaeologists were excavating a submerged Bronze Age village on the bottom of Lake Mezzano when they recovered the sword. In a statement, officials said the sword dates back to the 13th century B.C., during a period Italian archaeologists call the Recent Bronze Age — which is roughly equivalent to the Late Bronze Age. The sword "comes from an area of the southern shore of the lake that had previously seen limited investigation," officials said in a translated statement. Pictures released by officials show the dark, straight bronze blade resting on the rocky lake floor. REAL-LIFE EXCALIBUR? MAN ON A HIKE UNCOVERS GOLD SWORD RELIC HIDDEN UNDER TREE Officials also noted that the sword is so well-preserved that it "still features a sharp edge." The artifact "represents an important acquisition for understanding the communities that frequented the lake basin more than 3,000 years ago," the translated statement added. "It is the third sword found at the Mezzano site since the 1970s — a fact of extraordinary interest that confirms the exceptional archaeological importance of the context and offers new elements for exploring how the lake area was frequented and used during the Late Bronze Age," the statement added. Archaeologists also found axes, arrowheads, pins, spearheads and a razor — objects officials say appear to have been intentionally thrown in as part of a ritual or cultic practice. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "At Mezzano, the proximity between the recovered sword and a bronze razor is of particular interest, as it recalls associations documented in other Bronze Age contexts and attributable to individuals of high social status, likely belonging to warrior elites," the translated statement said. "Precisely for this reason, each new discovery takes on a value that goes well beyond the single object, contributing to the understanding of symbolic behaviors on the part of protohistoric communities," officials added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Archaeologists noted that the metal artifacts were found at remarkably consistent depths across the lakebed, helping them piece together how the objects ended up in the water. "Extending underwater stratigraphic excavation activities, integrated with the use of advanced technologies for documenting and spatially analyzing finds, will allow for a deeper understanding of the distribution of artifacts and the formation of the archaeological deposit," the statement added. Looking ahead, officials plan to continue underwater research at the lake while preparing an upcoming exhibition to display the bronze artifacts. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The Mezzano sword is the latest in a string of remarkable weapon discoveries across Europe. Earlier this summer, archaeologists in the Czech Republic announced the discovery of a Bronze Age hoard of intentionally damaged tools and weapons — including a sword blade struck apart with a single powerful blow. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At around the same time, a metal detectorist in northern Poland discovered a remarkably preserved, 2,700-year-old bronze sword standing upright in the ground.

articles.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
articles.summary: Prices are rising at their fastest pace for a year in the UK, and higher energy costs are on the way.
articles.body:
Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.

Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.

But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.

That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.

It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.

There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.

Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.

The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.

But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.

Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.

To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.

The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.

The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.

As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.

That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.

articles.title: ‘I’m not the same’: Mom must rebuild life for herself and daughter after Brooklyn collapse
articles.summary: After the deadly Brooklyn building collapse, all the belongings for Madelyn and her 2-year-old daughter are hanging in the balance.
articles.body: After the deadly Brooklyn building collapse, all the belongings for Madelyn and her 2-year-old daughter are hanging in the balance. So are their lives. The apartment where the mother and daughter lived was on the third floor of the Flatbush Avenue building that collapsed on Nov. 11. In an exclusive interview with Telemundo 47, Madelyn said she is grateful she was at work when the tragedy occurred, and her daughter was with her nanny. Now the goal for the mother, who immigrated to the U.S. from the Dominican Republic, is to move forward and recover what was lost. “I don’t know, because I had my life all set. I had my things,” the mother told Telemundo 47. “But it’s kind of left me, I don’t know, I feel like I’m not the same anymore, everything scares me.” The young mother visited the Dominican Republic’s consulate in New York City on Tuesday to request assistance. “We are now going to proceed with all the necessary paperwork for her and her family — cellphones, passports, and everything related to their documentation,” said Jesus Vasquez, the Consul General of the Dominican Republic in New York. “And we will be in contact with the Brooklyn Borough President to see how the borough can provide support, if not assistance, in conjunction with the Mayor here in the city.” Madelyn knows that, amidst everything, she was blessed. She mourns the deaths of eight of her neighbors in this tragedy, as she awaits help from authorities. “We, as the Dominican Consulate, have all the necessary information so that she can continue her life, since she has told us that she feels stable,” said Ramona Almonte, Director of Community Affairs at the Dominican Consulate in the city. “It doesn’t matter that she has a vulnerable immigration status; that doesn’t prevent us from reaching her. As the consul general told you, we will help her with all the support she needs.” Madelyn remains hopeful, even though her family is hundreds of miles away. “In whatever way I can [move on], since my family — I don’t have any family here, my family is all in the Dominican Republic,” she said.

articles.title: Stephen A Smith calls out critics demanding he fact-check Trump 'on the spot' in interviews
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith lambasted critics of his White House interview with President Donald Trump who claimed he didn't fact-check the president enough times.
articles.body: ESPN personality and "Straight Shooter" host Stephen A. Smith pushed back against critics Tuesday who accused him of not adequately fact-checking President Donald Trump during his White House interview last week. Smith said that though his interview had been largely well-received, some "people who have been in this industry before" have called him out for not pushing back against Trump. The sports host took issue with this critique by pointing out that the interview would not have happened had he focused on fact-checking the president. "You don't walk into the White House and talk to the president of the United States and plan on fact-checking him on the spot or interrupting him every sentence that he utters out of his mouth," Smith said. "You know why? Because you won't get through the damn interview. That's why." JOE ROGAN SAYS PODCASTERS HAVE NO BUSINESS AT TRUMP PRESS CONFERENCES ALONGSIDE REAL JOURNALISTS Smith noted that Trump often "filibusters," goes off track and embellishes his comments during interviews and calling them out would either take too much time or risk Trump ending the interview early. "I wanted to be able to challenge and push back in certain respects, but in the same breath, keep him in the damn chair because he does have the potential to just get up and walk off as he has done to people before," Smith said. Though he is not against pushing back against interviewees, including the president, Smith emphasized the need to pick and choose where to respond. THE ‘CROOKED’ CHARGE AGAINST NBC: WHY THE DONALD TRUMP-KRISTEN WELKER SLUGFEST WENT OFF THE RAILS "The goal, at least for me, is not to fact-check them on the spot in most instances," Smith said. "It's to make sure that they're quoted for the record, so we always have them on the record about what their positions are. That way, when we go back to double- and triple-check the facts, we're able to say, 'Hey, that wasn't true.'" Smith then spent the rest of the video fact-checking some of Trump's statements and urged people on both sides to "stop the BS." "Ladies and gentlemen, this is chess, it ain't checkers. articles.title: Woman says restaurant added unexpected 18% tip to $300 bill despite what menu stated
articles.summary: A New Jersey mother says an 18% tip on her family's $300-plus birthday dinner in Elizabeth wasn't disclosed, sparking a TikTok tipping debate. She spoke to Fox News Digital about it.
articles.body: A New Jersey woman who took her family out for a birthday dinner says the experience left a bad taste in her mouth — and it wasn't because of the food. Vanessa Cruz was celebrating her mother-in-law's birthday at a restaurant in Elizabeth, New Jersey, with her husband and two young children when she noticed an automatic 18% gratuity added to their bill of more than $300. The problem, according to Cruz, was that the restaurant's digital menu specified automatic gratuities applied to parties of six or more. RESTAURANT CHAIN MAY RETHINK CONTROVERSIAL 20% SERVICE CHARGE IN SOME VENUES AFTER CUSTOMER PUSHBACK Her family had only five people, including her 2-year-old son. When Cruz questioned the charge, the waitress explained the restaurant also automatically added 18% to bills exceeding $200 — a policy that Cruz said wasn't disclosed on the menu. "I think what peeved me the most was just the assumption that I have to give the 18% when it was already not part of that policy," Cruz told Fox News Digital. "It was just that, like, my choice of tipping was taken away from me, and it was more demanded," she added. CUSTOMER'S RESTAURANT RECEIPT SPARKS CONTROVERSY AFTER $6 CHARGE APPEARS FOR TO-GO BOX Cruz, a real estate agent who considers herself part of the service industry, emphasized she wasn't trying to avoid tipping altogether. She described the food as excellent but said the service was hardly exceptional. After requesting to speak to a manager, Cruz said she reiterated her concerns about the restaurant's seemingly inconsistent gratuity policy. She described the manager as courteous and professional, although the conversation didn't change the charge. Ultimately, her family paid the full 18% gratuity. "It wasn't for me to reduce the bill, right? It wasn't that I didn't want to pay anything," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Cruz subsequently shared her experience on TikTok, sparking a broader conversation about tipping expectations and whether customers should have the final say. "I think it's moved from an act of generosity to it's just a standard," she told Fox News Digital. "When did it become my problem?" Cruz also questioned why customers are increasingly expected to compensate for restaurant workers' low wages rather than businesses incorporating those costs into their prices. "I don't want to offend someone by saying it's not my problem. But when did it become my problem?" Cruz said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Many commenters on her TikTok post pointed out that servers aren't paid a livable wage, Cruz said. "Why aren't we asking restaurants to do that?" she said in response. Still, she acknowledged that serving large parties requires additional work and that automatic gratuities can be reasonable when clearly disclosed. As for whether she'd return to the restaurant, Cruz was doubtful, despite praising its food. Cruz indicated the issue ultimately comes down to transparency, fairness and respecting customers' choices. articles.title: US official says Hormuz insurance hits $64m: Is the strait really open?
articles.summary: Hung Cao says shipping insurance costs have soared to $64m for a single transit, challenging claims the strait is open.
articles.body:
A senior United States Navy official has claimed that insurance costs for commercial ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz have soared to $64m for a single transit, highlighting the enormous economic toll of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao made the remarks during a Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing on Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the cost of the war and its impact on freedom of navigation.

After the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, Iran in effect closed the strait, allowing only some ships to pass while targeting those it says are unauthorised. This has raised the risks for shipping in the strait exponentially and caused severe shortages of oil, gas, fertiliser and other essential products from Gulf producers usually shipped via this route.

Cao’s claim has not been independently verified and challenges previously reported rises in insurance costs over the course of the nine-month-old conflict.

The remarks come as US President Donald Trump insists that the military campaign against Iran is effectively over, and that the US Navy is successfully escorting ships through the strait, even as new attacks on oil tankers and continued restrictions on shipping raise questions about whether one of the world’s most important energy waterways is really open.

The strait, the only sea route from the Gulf to the Arabian Sea and the open ocean beyond, carried about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the war began.

Although some vessels are still navigating the waterway, shipping remains substantially below pre-war levels, while Iran and the US continue to impose competing restrictions.

What did Hung Cao say in the Senate hearing?

During an exchange with Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, Cao said insurance costs for commercial vessels had risen dramatically since the conflict began.

He initially cited an insurance cost of $54,000 for a single crossing before clarifying that that was what insurance had previously cost, before the war. The cost now, he said, stood at $64m.

Slotkin responded by blaming the war for the increase, arguing that commercial vessels no longer enjoyed the same freedom of navigation they had before the conflict.

Cao also detailed the strain the war has placed on the US Navy, including prolonged deployments, deteriorating conditions and pressure on military resources.

“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” he told lawmakers.

Democrats accused Cao of being a Trump “yes man” on the US-Israeli war on Iran, and downplaying its toll on sailors’ mental health after eight suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, asked him about a sailor who went overboard.

“Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself and he admitted that,” Cao told her, saying he used ‌a life preserver.

Gillibrand responded: “What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?”

“I think you are minimising what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand replied, while dismissing Cao’s response as “inhumane”.

Cao’s $64m figure appears unusually high, even by the standards of wartime shipping insurance.

There is no independently verified evidence that $64m is the current insurance premium for a regular commercial vessel crossing the volatile strait.

“He gave no context. Is he talking about additional premiums for war risk insurance which are set as a percentage of hull value?” Michelle Bockmann, an analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward, told Al Jazeera.

“If so, it depends on the vessel type and the rate paid in order to get proper perspective.”

In July, a report published by S&P Global said that war-risk insurance premiums had climbed to between 7.5 and 10 percent of a ship’s hull value, compared with 1 to 3 percent previously.

It estimated that insurance for a tanker carrying 270,000 metric tonnes of crude could, therefore, cost approximately $21m.

Separately, Reuters news agency reported in September that the cost of moving an oil cargo through Hormuz had risen to roughly $10m-$20m, quoting an executive at Dubai’s Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC).

Regardless of whether it now costs $20m or $60m for insurance to transit the Strait of Hormuz, premiums have surged because ships face the possibility of being struck by missiles, drones or naval mines while passing through the waterway.

War-risk insurance covers vessels against losses arising from military conflict. Its price depends on the value of the vessel, the cargo and the likelihood of an attack.

Higher insurance costs can also feed into freight rates, fuel prices and the cost of goods transported around the world.

Technically, yes. But it remains far from fully and freely open as it was before the war.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest weekly report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

The UKMTO recorded 308 vessel crossings during the seven days ending November 11, comprising 139 outbound and 169 inbound journeys.

Nevertheless, Trump has repeatedly suggested that Washington has secured shipping through the strait by providing naval escorts and maintaining the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Meanwhile, Iran insists that it, in fact, controls the passage of shipping through the strait.

Tehran has demanded that vessels use approved routes and coordinate with its forces. It has also announced exemptions for ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar.

The route approved by Iran takes ships much closer to its own coastline than they used to sail, as the map below shows:

The continuing dangers to ships ignoring Iran’s warnings were demonstrated this week.

On Monday, UKMTO reported two tanker attacks, including one near Oman that left a vessel disabled and its engine room on fire. The following day, Iranian forces claimed three additional tankers had struck naval mines.

On Tuesday, the US attacked targets on Iran’s Qeshm island , near Hormuz, following an Iranian drone attack targeting US military installations in Bahrain in recent days.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, said the strait could, therefore, hardly be considered open under normal circumstances.

“It is only open for business if mariners are prepared to take these risks, and it certainly isn’t open by any pre-war definition of the word,” he told Al Jazeera.

“It remains a miracle that we have avoided an energy crisis, and the longer this goes on, the more the alternatives will be developed.”

But Beauchamp said resolving the crisis would require Washington to confront the limits of its influence in the region.

“I can’t see a way that doesn’t involve conceding that the US does not have the ability to order things in the Middle East as it would wish,” he said.

articles.title: Intense rain and flooding hits both U.S. coasts, causing major issues in Florida
articles.summary: Florida’s east coast is being battered by heavy downpours as floodwaters rise in the southern part of the state, and the severe weather is expected to continue throughout the week.
articles.body: Florida’s east coast is being battered by heavy downpours as floodwaters rise in the southern part of the state, and the severe weather is expected to continue throughout the week. The rain started Tuesday in South Florida, with one round of heavy rain already in the Fort Lauderdale and Hollywood area. Radar estimates show 10 to 15 inches of rainfall, with rates as high as 3 inches per hour at times. By Wednesday morning, the heavy rain was expected to continue. Another foot of rain is possible before the weekend, with rainfall rates of up to 3 inches per hour in some areas. On Wednesday morning, the city of Hollywood urged residents to shelter in place. Around 11 million people from Miami to Jacksonville are at risk of flooding. In Melbourne, some waited in bumper-to-bumper traffic for hours to secure sandbags. Generally, 4 to 6 inches of rain are expected, with totals expected to reach 8 to 12 inches, or higher, locally. Intense rainfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour are possible. The St. Johns River is already at a major flood stage. Urban flash flooding and river flooding will be likely as the storm continues. Broward County closed schools Wednesday, including before- and after-school care programs and extracurricular activities. The district has not yet announced whether schools will be closed at all later this week. Miami-Dade Public Schools are staying open Wednesday, but the district said in a social media post that it would be flexible with tardiness due to the weather. The roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood partially collapsed, according to video from NBC 6 South Florida. And Memorial Regional Hospital, also in Hollywood, suspended visitation for the day. Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport issued a ground stop around 9:30 a.m. Wednesday, and it was expected to stay in effect until at least 10:45 a.m. The latest batch of rains come just weeks after the region saw a 1- in-1,000-year rain event that similarly brought heavy rain and flooding. “I think everyone learned their lesson,” Christian Greene told NBC News. “No one wants to do that again.” Videos from Hollywood show cars stuck and submerged — with some people abandoning their vehicles in the mess. Water was seen rushing through neighborhoods elsewhere, and residents were forced to drive through floods overnight. An NBC News-verified social media video shows hail falling in Fort Lauderdale on Tuesday night. Maj. Jason Drinkwater with the Brevard County Sheriff’s Office called the preparations “precautionary.” “People are losing their homes. They’re losing a lot of their personal belongings in their homes, and obviously they want to protect that,” Drinkwater said. Threat of dangerous waves Heavy rains and gusty winds are hitting northern California this morning, from Redding to San Francisco, and heavy rain will spread south throughout Wednesday. Winter weather alerts are in place for 1 million people, 12 million are under flood alerts and 9 million are facing wind alerts. Dangerous waves, flooding and strong winds are expected, along with power outages. Both Los Angeles and the Bay Area could see 1 to 3 inches of rain locally, with 3 to 5 inches in the mountains. Rates of 3 inches per hour are expected. The soaking rain will move through California om Wednesday, with an elevated flood risk along the coast. The Sierra Nevada is also facing the potential for some heavy snow this week, with up to 4 feet expected on the mountain passes. Heavy snow will blanket the Sierra into tonight. On Thursday, the storm will move east, bringing rain and snow to the Great Basin region, while snow continues over the Sierra Nevada.

articles.body: Hollywood actor Hugh Jackman, Kevin Parker and over 150 other Australian artists and entertainers have joined a campaign to protect Scott Reef from Woodside Energy’s proposed gas drilling project. In an open letter to Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt, they urged the government to reject the plans and protect the marine environment surrounding the reef off Western Australia’s Kimberley coast.According to Greenpeace, Woodside plans to drill up to 57 wells for its Browse gas project, about 270 kilometres from the Kimberley coast. The project is forecast to produce 1.6 billion tonnes of climate pollution and carries the risk of a catastrophic oil spill along endangered whale migration routes. Scott Reef supports thousands of species, including endangered whales and vulnerable turtles.More than 150 artists sign open letter opposing Woodside’s Scott Reef projectThe open letter asks Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt to reject Woodside’s oil and gas drilling plans at Scott Reef. Reportedly, more than 150 Australian entertainers and creatives have signed. The signatories include 2026 ARIA nominees Kevin Parker of Tame Impala, Tkay Maidza and G Flip. Actors Hugh Jackman and Simon Baker have also added their names, alongside musicians Tina Arena and Paul Kelly.Reportedly, the letter calls for protection of Australia’s largest oceanic reef system. It places the proposed Browse gas project at the centre of concerns about the future of the reef and the marine life that depends on it.Why are Australian artists concerned about Woodside’s plans for Scott ReefWoodside’s Browse gas project would involve drilling up to 57 wells under and around Scott Reef, according to the campaign. The reef lies 270 kilometres from the Kimberley coast of Western Australia. Reportedly, the project is forecast to emit 1.6 billion tonnes of climate pollution. It also warned of the risk of a catastrophic oil spill in pathways used by endangered whales during migration.The proposed drilling has become the focus of the open letter signed by Australian artists and creatives. Their appeal is directed at Environment Minister Murray Watt, asking him to reject the plans. The letter links the project’s potential effects with the need to protect the reef and its surrounding marine environment.Singer-songwriter Missy Higgins, who signed the open letter, said, “Scott Reef is an ancient coral reef off WA’s Kimberley coast, home to endangered whales, vulnerable turtles and hundreds of other marine species. Woodside’s plans to drill up to 57 wells under and around it put this extraordinary place at risk. We need to preserve these beautiful places for our kids. If not now, then when?”Australian singers share concerns over Woodside’s plans for Scott ReefSeveral signatories explained why they supported the appeal. Musician Jessica Mauboy said, “Caring for Country means caring for our oceans and all the life they hold. Places like Scott Reef are precious, and we have a responsibility to protect them for future generations. I’m adding my voice to the call to protect Scott Reef and keep it safe from gas drilling.”Singer-songwriter Sarah Blasko also opposed a major new gas project at the reef. She said, “Scott Reef off Western Australia’s Kimberley Coast is not the place for a massive new gas project by Woodside. It’s our responsibility to protect our beautiful reefs and rare marine life. They are, after all, what this country is best known for around the world. If we don’t protect them, what does it say about us to our children and the world?”Disclaimer: This article is based on information published by Greenpeace, including its open letter and campaign statements. articles.title: National security and AI figures urge DOJ to probe what Nvidia knew about chip smuggling
articles.summary: A letter from 15 national security and AI leaders scrutinized the chipmaker’s knowledge of illegal transfers of its chips to China.
articles.body: A group of 15 national security experts and AI policy leaders is urging the Justice Department to investigate what Nvidia knew about the alleged smuggling of its advanced AI chips to China, and whether the company continued doing business with customers after evidence emerged that they were illegally diverting the technology. The letter, sent Tuesday and addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche, asks the department to examine whether Nvidia kept selling chips to customers or middlemen after receiving evidence that they were illegally routing them to China, or whether the company “deliberately blinded itself to export control violations.” “The United States has the world’s most advanced SI chip technology, much of it built by Nvidia,” the letter states, using the Trump administration’s “super intelligence” label for AI. “Smuggling operations threaten to undermine that lead, giving China access to hardware necessary for developing advanced SI and deploying it to boost its military capabilities and international influence.” The 15 signatories include a range of national security experts and AI policy specialists, such as David Buckley, the Central Intelligence Agency’s former inspector general; Randy Manner, a retired Army general; Chris McGuire, a former Biden official who specialized in chips; and Brad Carson, the president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, the AI advocacy group that organized the letter. “China and our competitors around the world have their sights set on our advanced AI chips so they can build up their AI capabilities,” Carson told NBC News. “Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are at the top of their wish lists.” Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. On Tuesday, the company’s board of directors announced that it would establish a committee dedicated to investigating national security and export control compliance. In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson said: “As a general policy, the Department doesn’t discuss the details or existence of ongoing investigations, but it goes without saying that any investigation by the DOJ is based in evidence and facts.” The letter comes amid growing scrutiny of the American chipmaker and calls from Congress to investigate the extent of Nvidia’s awareness of the chips’ destination and whether the company did anything about potential smuggling. On Tuesday, the Justice and Commerce departments shared details about their investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean company tied to suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang. Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang is alleged to have had an affair with Megaspeed’s Huang. Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China. In a joint statement Tuesday, the agencies said Commerce opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, requested sales records from Nvidia in May 2025 and that Nvidia placed the company on its no-sell list the following month. Commerce investigators also conducted an in-person inspection of Megaspeed’s facilities with Singaporean law enforcement in June 2025. A source familiar with the matter said that Nvidia itself is not the target of any existing investigation related to national security. The Justice Department said it took the lead in the criminal investigation after that enforcement action. The agencies said they would continue working together to pursue any criminal conduct that may have occurred. Huang has agreed to sit for an interview with several national security-focused House committees on Dec. 1, according to House Republicans. The appearance will focus on the former CEO’s role in “a potential breach of our national security,” according to the lawmakers. Tuesday’s letter to Blanche points to several smuggling cases the Justice Department has brought in the past year involving Nvidia. In March 2026, prosecutors charged three people in an alleged scheme in which a Southeast Asian intermediary bought roughly $2.5 billion worth of servers containing advanced AI chips. Prosecutors allege at least $510 million worth were illegally sent to China. “Repeated attempts to route Nvidia chips to China point to a pattern that warrants a closer examination of company practices and how Nvidia responded to repeated alarming discoveries over the past several years regarding the scale of smuggling operations,” the letter states. Smuggled chips are estimated to equal at least 25% of the chips Chinese AI companies obtained through legal routes — though the actual figure may be far larger. Many Chinese companies, including tech titans Alibaba and Tencent, have reportedly also leased chips from data centers based in Singapore, Malaysia and other southeast Asian countries. This week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced that it would close that loophole. The department said it would enact a new set of regulations limiting foreign data centers’ ability to rent their chips to Chinese companies and enacting new requirements for chip customers in five southeast Asian countries — including Singapore and Malaysia — in order to receive chips from American companies like Nvidia or AMD. China criticized the rule. “Such actions run counter to the consensus reached between the two sides, infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises, and disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing in Beijing. Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips are widely considered the most powerful available. Under current export rules, Nvidia cannot sell its top-tier chips to China, though it can sell older generation chips, from the H200 family, to China with a 25% fee taken by the White House. The Justice Department established a new body dedicated to cracking down on AI-related crime in early November. This force, called the Super Intelligence Task Force, aims to “ensure that America’s leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct,” according to the Department. Some lawmakers have clamored for stricter rules on advanced AI chip exports to China. Members of the House’s Select Committee on China have sought to restrict China’s ability to purchase chipmaking equipment and to implement stronger chip-tracking technology — to ensure that chips sent to data centers outside mainland China remain outside of the country. Tuesday’s letter closes by urging the department “to follow the evidence wherever it leads and pursue appropriate enforcement action where violations are established.”

articles.title: Mullin appears for congressional hearing after historic nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: The committee's focus is to be on worldwide threats since the Sept. 11 attacks.
articles.body:
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is on Capitol Hill on Wednesday to talk about worldwide threats since Sept. 11, 2001, but he's likely to be in the hot seat over questions about technology issues that disrupted millions of Americans over the last week.

Mullin is testifying before the House Committee on Homeland Security for a hearing underway titled "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" along with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia.

Mullin is expected to be grilled over the investigation into last Friday's rare nationwide ground stop , the second since 9/11. This ground stop stranded millions of passengers going into last weekend.

He is also expected to receive questions about the cyber outages that have affected airlines, Microsoft Outlook, banks and other services.

Mullin has repeatedly assured the public that Friday's air traffic incident, in which flights were grounded for four hours, was not nefarious and echoed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on what caused the disruption.

Duffy told ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that work was being performed to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred.

The ground stop was issued after the installation of a Juniper router at the Arkansas facility flooded the network with data, overwhelming an older system and resulting in telecommunications issues, according to officials.

Duffy told reporters on Tuesday that the FAA had spent a year testing the routers and that the issue occurred on the 69th installation.

Mullin told CNBC in an interview on Tuesday that "the FAA issue was because they're working on 50-year-old equipment with copper wire, that should be fiber."

He also stressed that the U.S. is not under attack.

"There's no cyber threat that's taking place. The homeland is very secure," he said.

Mullin could also face questions about his trip to Louisiana on Saturday to attend the Texas-LSU college football game while thousands of flights were still disrupted from the ground stop the day before.

The secretary told CNBC he would not have flown if the airways weren't open.

"And we still got to live our life at the same time," he added.

articles.title: Happy International Men’s Day 2026: Top 50 Wishes, Messages and Quotes to share with your loved ones

articles.body: Some of the most important people in our lives never ask to be thanked. Men are those important people in our lives whose presence is just as important as they are.They fix the leaking tap, drive through traffic to reach the school gate, and say "I'm fine" when they are anything but that. They carry their worries quietly, because somewhere along the way they learned that men are meant to be solid walls, not open windows.International Men's Day is a small chance to change that belief. It is a day to say thank you out loud, and to say something just as important that ‘you don't have to carry everything alone. Men are allowed to feel tired, to ask for help, to be gentle, and to be celebrated for it.’Kind words may seem like a tiny gift, yet most of us remember the ones we received for years. A single message can make a father, brother, friend, partner or colleague feel truly seen.When is International Men’s Day celebrated?International Men's Day is marked every year on 19 November, and this year it falls on a Thursday. The first 19 November observance as Men’s Day was held in 1999 in Trinidad and Tobago by Dr Jerome Teelucksingh, who picked his father's birthday as the date.Here are some heartfelt quotes, wishes and messages to celebrate the men in your lifeHappy International Men's Day 2026: Top 50 wishes, messages and quotes to share with your loved onesHappy Men's Day to the men who make life warmer, brighter and more meaningful for all of us.Wishing every man strength, kindness, and peace of mind today and always.May you keep inspiring others with your courage and your compassion.To the men who stay strong through hard times: your resilience truly deserves admiration.Here's to men who lead with wisdom and act with honesty.Today we celebrate your patience, your perseverance, and your steady presence.Wishing every wonderful man happiness, success, and good emotional health.Thank you for being caring, dependable, and supportive. Happy Men's Day!May your day be full of positivity and recognition for everything you do.Keep shining with confidence and kindness. articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least five people
articles.summary: Most of the casualties were in strikes on Odesa that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as ‘brutal’.
articles.body:
Russian air attacks across Ukraine have killed at least five people, authorities said, a day after a Ukrainian strike on Russia’s Kerch Bridge killed two and caused part of the structure to collapse.

In the southern city of Odesa, at least four people were killed and 13 others wounded in Russian air strikes, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the “brutal and deliberate” attack also targeted first responders.

Oleg Kiper, the head of the Odesa region’s military administration, said three Russian strikes hit the city’s “historic centre”. Odesa city council said one of the strikes hit a UNESCO-protected area, causing a car to catch fire and blowing out hundreds of windows in at least seven buildings.

Ukrainian emergency services shared images showing wounded people on stretchers, buildings with shattered windows and firefighters extinguishing a blaze on a rooftop.

“There were double-tap strikes after first responders and police officers had already arrived at the scene,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.

He said the attack served as “further proof of what the Russians really want and how they truly regard diplomatic efforts”.

In the southeastern Zaporizhia region, a Russian drone strike killed a woman and injured a man in the town of Kushuhum, local military administration official Mykhailo Semykin said.

Attacks on the region also forced local authorities to order families with children to leave the village of Balabyne, he said.

“We are talking about 85 children from 80 families. In total, the evacuation affects 184 people,” he wrote on Telegram.

In northern Ukraine’s Rivne region, 80 settlements were left without electricity after a Russian attack, authorities said. No deaths or injuries were reported.

Ukraine’s Energy Ministry says Russia has launched more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September. New power outages had been recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, Sumy, Rivne, and Cherkasy regions in the last 24 hours, Interfax reported on Wednesday. Russia has increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the lead-up to winter, in a strategy the United Nations said amounted to war crimes.

“The situation in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions remains extremely difficult. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power supply as soon as possible, but repeated attacks are significantly complicating repair work,” Ukraine’s energy ministry said.

The attacks came a day after Ukraine attacked Russia’s Kerch Bridge – a symbolic road-and-rail link from Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula – killing two people.

As the warring sides continue to trade long-range attacks, the European Commission has proposed a new 45 billion euro ($49.5bn) loan to Ukraine to help fill a 70 billion euro ($76.8bn) funding gap for next year.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused since it launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

“We very much hope for the swift adoption of this decision by the European Parliament and the Council and count on the support of all EU member states,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Although Ukraine is not officially on the agenda during a tripartite meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Beijing, the talks are being watched closely in the Ukrainian capital.

Reporting from Kyiv on Wednesday, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said there were concerns in Ukraine that the meeting “could place the Russian President in a similar category of world powers and world leaders as the United States and China and what the optics mean for Ukraine”.

MacAlpine said parallel meetings to negotiate the end of the Ukraine war were due to begin in Berlin on Thursday. “The US delegates are reportedly travelling there to meet with the Ukrainian delegation, potentially with some of the leaders of Europe,” she said.

The agenda is expected to address Ukrainian demands for security guarantees and the prisoner swap agreed in Abu Dhabi last week, MacAlpine said.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries formally nominated as first Black US House speaker
articles.summary: The New York congressman is nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in this month’s midterm elections.
articles.body:
Washington, DC, United States – Hakeem Jeffries has become the first Black lawmaker officially nominated for speaker of the US House of Representatives, marking a milestone in the country’s political history.

In a closed-door vote on Wednesday, the 56-year-old New York congressman secured his party’s nomination for the post just weeks after Democrats scored sweeping victories in the midterm elections, reclaiming control of both chambers of the US Congress.

Before the vote, Jeffries confirmed plans to force members of his party to take a recorded vote amid growing dissent among progressives over his leadership.

Some of those members, most of whom were elected this month, declined to say whether they would support Jeffries. Several said they wanted a leader who would support bold, populist policies they had campaigned on.

One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.

“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.

Jeffries has received pushback within some Democratic circles over his record on Israel and ties to pro-Israel lobbying groups, like AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. During an interview with The Atlantic magazine on Tuesday, Jeffries addressed some of that criticism, calling for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and a two-state solution.

Despite some opposition in Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries received overwhelming support from the House Democratic Caucus with 251 members voting to back his candidacy. Only 11 members opposed it.

Just before the vote, Jeffries took to social media to post a Bible verse from the book of Corinthians reading,” For we walk by faith, not by sight.”

In 2023, Jeffries was put forward by Democrats as their pick to succeed former US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, who was ousted by his fellow Republicans in favour of the chamber’s current speaker, Mike Johnson. Wednesday’s vote, however, means Jeffries has now been formally nominated by members of his party.

Jeffries is poised to replace Johnson as speaker when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3 with a Democratic majority and a vote on the new speaker is held in the full chamber.
